stories.title: Caliphs, Amirs and Sultans: Who Ruled Baghdad
stories.blurb: Five centuries of power in the Abbasid capital: a caliph's round city, a family purge, a brothers' war, a flight to Samarra, Persian and Turkish protectors, and the Mongol end.

steps.name: Al-Mansur founds the Round City
steps.what: The second Abbasid caliph built a walled circular capital on the Tigris with his palace and mosque at its centre.
steps.why: A new dynasty needed a capital away from the Syrian Umayyad heartland and the restive garrison city of Kufa.

steps.name: Harun destroys the Barmakids
steps.what: Harun had his vizier Ja'far executed and the rest of the family imprisoned.
steps.why: It showed that even the most powerful administrators held office only at the caliph's pleasure.

steps.name: Siege of Baghdad in the brothers' war
steps.what: Al-Ma'mun's generals besieged al-Amin for a year; the city was battered and al-Amin was killed.
steps.why: The first great civil war of Abbasid Baghdad decided the succession and wrecked the Round City.

steps.name: Al-Ma'mun comes home to Baghdad
steps.what: After ruling from Merv, al-Ma'mun entered Baghdad and made it the capital again.
steps.why: His arrival ended a rebellion by Baghdadis who had set up a rival caliph.

steps.name: The mihna: an inquisition over the Quran
steps.what: Scholars were made to declare the Quran created; Ibn Hanbal refused and was flogged.
steps.why: The caliphs lost the contest to define doctrine, and religious authority passed to the scholars.

steps.name: Al-Mu'tasim moves to Samarra
steps.what: Clashes between Turkish soldiers and Baghdadis led the caliph to build a new capital upriver.
steps.why: For over fifty years the court lived among its slave soldiers rather than its subjects.

steps.name: Murder of al-Mutawakkil and the anarchy
steps.what: Turkish officers killed the caliph, opening nine years in which commanders made and unmade caliphs.
steps.why: Real power had passed to the army that was supposed to protect the caliph.

steps.name: A caliph besieged in Baghdad
steps.what: Al-Musta'in fled to Baghdad and was besieged there by the army of al-Mu'tazz from Samarra.
steps.why: Baghdad and Samarra fought each other as rival centres of power.

steps.name: Caliphs return to Baghdad
steps.what: Al-Mu'tadid settled the court in palaces on the east bank of Baghdad.
steps.why: A brief Abbasid revival restored Baghdad as the seat of government.

steps.name: The Buyids take Baghdad
steps.what: A Shi'i Daylamite dynasty from Iran took the city and soon blinded the caliph.
steps.why: The caliph became a figurehead under foreign military protectors for a century.

steps.name: Tughril the Seljuk enters Baghdad
steps.what: The Seljuk Turks replaced the Buyids and styled themselves defenders of the Sunni caliph.
steps.why: A new Turkish sultanate ruled in the caliph's name.

steps.name: Al-Basasiri prays for the Fatimids
steps.what: A rebel commander had Friday prayers said in Baghdad for the Fatimid caliph of Cairo for a year.
steps.why: For a moment Baghdad looked set to fall to the rival Ismaili caliphate.

steps.name: Al-Nasir revives the caliphate
steps.what: With the Seljuks gone, al-Nasir ruled Iraq himself and used futuwwa brotherhoods to bind princes to him.
steps.why: It was the last flowering of Abbasid political power.

steps.name: The Mongols take Baghdad
steps.what: Hulagu besieged and stormed the city, sacked it and executed the last caliph.
steps.why: The Abbasid caliphate of Baghdad ended after five centuries.

stories.title: Paper, Translators and Colleges in Baghdad
stories.blurb: How cheap paper, Greek translations, booksellers and endowed colleges made Baghdad the centre of learning, until the libraries burned.

steps.name: Paper making comes to Baghdad
steps.what: Paper mills were set up in Baghdad under Barmakid patronage.
steps.why: Cheap paper made bureaucracy, bookselling and scholarship possible on a new scale.

steps.name: Al-Khwarizmi writes al-Jabr
steps.what: Al-Khwarizmi wrote his book on solving equations, dedicated to al-Ma'mun.
steps.why: It gave the world algebra and spread Indian numerals westward.

steps.name: The House of Wisdom under al-Ma'mun
steps.what: The palace library became a centre for copying and translation.
steps.why: Caliphal money paid for Greek, Persian and Indian knowledge to be put into Arabic.

steps.name: Hunayn ibn Ishaq translates Galen
steps.what: Hunayn and his circle translated Galen, Hippocrates and other Greek works.
steps.why: Their versions became the basis of medicine in the Islamic world and Europe.

steps.name: Al-Kindi, philosopher of the Arabs
steps.what: Al-Kindi adapted Greek philosophy to Islamic questions.
steps.why: He started the tradition of Arabic philosophy.

steps.name: The Banu Musa's Book of Ingenious Devices
steps.what: Three brothers described automata, valves and trick vessels.
steps.why: It showed the practical side of Baghdad's scientific patronage.

steps.name: Al-Adudi Hospital opens
steps.what: The Buyid ruler founded a large staffed hospital.
steps.why: Hospitals became teaching institutions as well as charities.

steps.name: Ibn al-Nadim catalogues all books
steps.what: A bookseller compiled the Fihrist, listing books known in Arabic.
steps.why: It records the size of the Baghdad book trade, much of it now lost.

steps.name: A public library in al-Karkh
steps.what: A Buyid vizier endowed a library open to scholars.
steps.why: Endowed libraries spread learning beyond the court.

steps.name: The Nizamiyya opens
steps.what: The Seljuk vizier opened an endowed college with salaried teachers and student stipends.
steps.why: It became the model of the madrasa across the Islamic world.

steps.name: Al-Ghazali teaches and leaves
steps.what: Al-Ghazali attacked the philosophers, then left Baghdad to seek Sufi certainty.
steps.why: His work shaped Sunni thought for centuries.

steps.name: The Mustansiriyya opens
steps.what: A caliphal college for all four Sunni law schools opened by the Tigris.
steps.why: The building still stands, the finest relic of Abbasid Baghdad.

steps.name: Al-Wasiti paints the Maqamat
steps.what: A scribe illustrated al-Hariri's stories with lively scenes of daily life.
steps.why: It is among the masterpieces of Arabic book painting.

steps.name: The libraries are destroyed
steps.what: The Mongol sack destroyed Baghdad's libraries and colleges.
steps.why: Baghdad lost its role as the centre of Arabic learning.
